Every request to a CORI data bucket is written to an S3 server access log.
This resource turns those logs into charts: who is downloading what, from
which bucket, and how that changes over time.

Code cells are set `eval: false` in the document front matter because
rendering them queries several months of live log data. Run them
interactively against a real window.

## Where the logs live

Server access logging is enabled on every allowlisted bucket except
`cori.data.verse`, which is the destination. Log objects land under a
date-partitioned prefix that encodes both the source bucket and the day:

```
s3://cori.data.verse/logs/312512371189/us-east-1/<bucket>/YYYY/MM/DD/<file>
```

That layout matters for performance. Narrowing the glob to the months you
care about is what keeps a query reading megabytes instead of the full
history — there are hundreds of thousands of small log objects.

```{r}
#| label: libraries
#| cache: false

library(cori.data.s3)
library(cori.charts)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

library(noctua)

load_fonts()
update_cori_geom_defaults()

# Every cached chunk is keyed on today's date and the installed cori.charts
# build, so results expire nightly and when the theme package is reinstalled.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(cache.extra = list(
  as.character(Sys.Date()),
  as.character(utils::packageDescription("cori.charts")$Built)
))
```

## Reading the logs

Queries run against the Athena table `cori_data_monitoring.s3_access_logs`,
which sits over the same raw log objects but is partition-projected on
`sourcebucket/year/month/day`. Parsing happens server-side in Athena rather
than in R.

This matters more than it sounds. Parsing the raw objects directly from R
took **93 minutes for a 30-day window**, 85 of them on `cori.data.fcc`
alone. The cost is driven by log *object count*, not data volume — roughly
a million objects a month at ~4 KB each. Athena's partition projection skips
that enumeration entirely.

Caller classification comes from the view
`cori_data_monitoring.s3_access_identified`, which resolves four generations
of vended session-name format into a single `caller_class` / `caller_id`
pair. Keeping that logic in one view is deliberate: this document and
`reports.sql` previously carried two hand-maintained parsers that disagreed
about the same rows.

### A word on what `api_calls` counts

It counts S3 API calls, **not downloads**. DuckDB and other range-reading
clients fetch a parquet file in many HTTP 206 range requests. Measured over
30 days, 99.3% of `cori.data.fcc`'s anonymous GETs are range reads —
1,931,764 API calls against just 13,563 distinct objects, a 142x inflation.
Other buckets are essentially unaffected.

So `distinct_objects` and `bytes_sent` are the defensible usage measures.
`api_calls` is kept because it is what the log actually records, but it
should never be described as a download count.

```{r}
#| label: read

con <- DBI::dbConnect(
  noctua::athena(),
  schema_name    = "cori_data_monitoring",
  s3_staging_dir = Sys.getenv(
    "CORI_ATHENA_STAGING",
    "s3://aws-athena-query-results-312512371189-us-east-1/cori-data-monitoring/"
  )
)
# Aggregated server-side; only the summary crosses the wire. The date
# predicate is written against the concatenated partition columns rather
# than a derived date, which is what lets Athena prune partitions before
# scanning (see the header of cori.data/src/athena/reports.sql).
activity <- DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT
      sourcebucket                                          AS bucket,
      from_iso8601_date(year || '-' || month || '-' || day) AS day,
      caller_class,
      CASE WHEN caller_class = 'vended_tagged'
           THEN 'tag-' || caller_id ELSE caller_id END      AS caller,
      COUNT(*)                            AS api_calls,
      COUNT(DISTINCT key)                 AS distinct_objects,
      SUM(TRY_CAST(bytessent AS BIGINT))  AS bytes
  FROM cori_data_monitoring.s3_access_identified
  WHERE operation LIKE 'REST.GET.OBJECT%'
    AND (year || month || day) >= date_format(current_date - interval '30' day, '%Y%m%d')
  GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4
") |>
  # Athena BIGINT arrives as bit64::integer64, which scales::label_bytes() and
  # label_comma() cannot format.
  mutate(across(c(api_calls, distinct_objects, bytes), as.numeric))

# Not on.exit(): at top level of a knitr chunk it fires immediately after
# that one expression, closing the connection before the query runs.
DBI::dbDisconnect(con)

glimpse(activity)
```

One row per bucket, day, caller class, and caller. Everything below is
`dplyr` on that frame — the expensive work is already done.

## API calls over time, by bucket

```{r}
#| label: chart-by-bucket

week <- activity |>
  filter(day >= Sys.Date() - 7, day < Sys.Date()) |>
  group_by(bucket, day) |>
  summarise(api_calls = sum(api_calls), .groups = "drop")

# The four busiest buckets carry colour; the rest stay as gray context.
top_buckets <- week |>
  group_by(bucket) |>
  summarise(api_calls = sum(api_calls), .groups = "drop") |>
  slice_max(api_calls, n = 4, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  pull(bucket)
bucket_colors <- setNames(
  unname(cori_colors[c("Emerald", "Mid Blue", "Mid Purple", "Mid Orange")]),
  top_buckets
)
end_labels <- week |>
  filter(bucket %in% top_buckets, day == max(day))
top_share <- sum(week$api_calls[week$bucket == top_buckets[1]]) / sum(week$api_calls)

ggplot(week, aes(day, api_calls, group = bucket)) +
  geom_line(
    data      = filter(week, !bucket %in% top_buckets),
    color     = cori_colors[["CORI Gray"]],
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data      = filter(week, bucket %in% top_buckets),
    aes(color = bucket),
    linewidth = 1.5
  ) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
    data         = end_labels,
    aes(label = bucket, color = bucket),
    hjust        = 0,
    nudge_x      = 0.3,
    direction    = "y",
    size         = 4.5,
    family       = "Lato",
    fontface     = "bold",
    segment.size = 0
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = bucket_colors) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_comma(),
    limits = c(0, NA),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    date_labels = "%b %d",
    breaks      = sort(unique(week$day)),
    expand      = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.3))
  ) +
  theme_cori_line() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(
    title    = paste0(
      top_buckets[1], " drives ", percent(top_share, accuracy = 1),
      " of the\nweek's S3 API calls"
    ),
    subtitle = "Daily GET API calls by bucket over the past week; the four busiest are highlighted",
    caption  = paste0(
      "Source: CORI analysis of S3 server access logs (cori_data_monitoring.s3_access_identified).\n",
      "Range reads inflate API call counts; see the note above. Excludes today, which is not yet logged."
    ),
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  )
```

## Who is downloading

`caller_class` separates four things the previous version of this document
collapsed into one:

| class | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `anonymous_unauth` | no credential at all — `requester` is `-` |
| `local_iam` | a known IAM user or role, not via the vending endpoint |
| `other_assumed_role` | an assumed role unrelated to vending (e.g. AWS Config) |
| `vended_*` | a credential from the vending endpoint |

That split matters. Measured over 30 days, `anonymous_unauth` is 91.98% of
all GETs and `vended_*` is 0.01% — 209 requests. Folding them together, as
this document used to, hid the fact that essentially nobody uses the vending
endpoint while the overwhelming majority of consumption carries no identity
at all.

A `vended_tagged` caller is **self-declared**. The `caller` parameter is an
unvalidated query string on a public, unauthenticated endpoint, so treat it
as a usage label, never as an identity.

```{r}
#| label: chart-by-caller

class_phrase <- c(
  anonymous_unauth   = "Anonymous callers",
  local_iam          = "Staff IAM callers",
  other_assumed_role = "Infrastructure roles",
  "vended_*"         = "Vended-credential callers"
)
class_colors <- c(
  anonymous_unauth   = cori_colors[["Emerald"]],
  local_iam          = cori_colors[["Mid Blue"]],
  other_assumed_role = cori_colors[["Mid Orange"]],
  "vended_*"         = cori_colors[["Mid Purple"]]
)
fmt_bytes <- function(x) {
  v <- vapply(x / 1e6, function(m) {
    if (is.na(m)) "NA"
    else if (m == 0) "0"
    else if (m < 0.01) "<0.01"
    else format(signif(m, 3), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
  }, character(1))
  paste(v, "MB")
}

by_caller <- activity |>
  filter(day >= Sys.Date() - 7) |>
  mutate(caller_class = ifelse(grepl("^vended", caller_class), "vended_*", caller_class)) |>
  group_by(caller_class, caller) |>
  summarise(bytes = sum(bytes, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

by_class <- by_caller |>
  group_by(caller_class) |>
  summarise(bytes = sum(bytes), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(bytes))

by_caller |>
  slice_max(bytes, n = 12, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ggplot(aes(reorder(caller, bytes), bytes, fill = caller_class)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = fmt_bytes(bytes)),
    hjust    = -0.15,
    fontface = "bold",
    family   = "Lato",
    size     = 4
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = class_colors, labels = class_phrase) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  theme_cori_horizontal_bars() +
  theme(legend.position = "top") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 1)) +
  labs(
    title    = paste0(
      class_phrase[[by_class$caller_class[1]]], " account for ",
      percent(by_class$bytes[1] / sum(by_class$bytes), accuracy = 1),
      "\nof bytes served"
    ),
    subtitle = "Twelve largest callers by bytes sent over the past week, colored by caller class",
    caption  = paste0(
      "Source: CORI analysis of S3 server access logs (cori_data_monitoring.s3_access_identified).\n",
      "Bytes rather than API calls, which range reads inflate. Caller resolved by the s3_access_identified view."
    ),
    x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL
  )
```

### Is a name on this chart an IAM user?

Not necessarily. Take a caller labelled `tag-bench`. It is not an IAM user:
the log's `requester` field for those requests names a shared role, not a
user, and reads:

```
arn:aws:sts::312512371189:assumed-role/CoriDataVendCredentials-CoriDataS3ReaderRole…/coridata-tag-bench-1792415554
```

That ARN has three parts:

- `assumed-role/CoriDataVendCredentials-CoriDataS3ReaderRole…` is the one
  shared role that every vended credential assumes. It says nothing about
  who is using it.
- `coridata-tag-` marks the session as tagged, so the view classifies it as
  `vended_tagged`.
- `bench` is the tag, and `1792415554` is the epoch second at which the
  session started (2026-10-19 13:12:34 UTC). The query above shows it in
  the `caller` column as `tag-bench`, keeping the `tag-` prefix so a label
  is never mistaken for an IAM user name.

The tag is whatever the caller passed as `caller = "bench"` when it asked
the vending endpoint for a credential. The endpoint is public and does not
check it, so `tag-bench` is a self-declared label. Two people can use the same
tag, and one person can use many. A tag is good for grouping one pipeline's
traffic, and it is not evidence of who ran it. When it was seen, `bench`
made 7 sessions on 2026-10-19, all against `cori.data.fcc`, and one of them
moved 98.9% of the bytes.

Compare a `local_iam` caller, such as a staff member's email address. There
the `requester` is `arn:aws:iam::312512371189:user/<name>`, which AWS fills
in itself and the caller cannot choose, so it does identify who made the
request. The same applies to untagged vended callers, which carry
`ip:<8 hex characters>`, the first eight characters of a SHA-256 hash of the
caller's IP address, so they separate networks without naming anyone.

So the colour of the bar tells you what kind of name you are looking at: a
`local_iam` name can be looked up in IAM, and a `vended_*` name cannot. To
learn more about a vended label, filter the log on its `caller_id` and read
the `remoteip`, `useragent` and object keys.

## Year-to-date summary

```{r}
#| label: ytd

activity |>
  filter(day >= as.Date(format(Sys.Date(), "%Y-01-01"))) |>
  group_by(bucket) |>
  summarise(
    api_calls = sum(api_calls),
    objects   = sum(distinct_objects),
    mb        = round(sum(bytes, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e6, 1),
    callers   = n_distinct(caller),
    .groups   = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(mb)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Swap the `filter()` for `day >= Sys.Date() - 90` to get the trailing
ninety days instead.

## Caveats

Server access logging is best effort. Most requests produce a record and
most records arrive within a few hours, but delivery is neither guaranteed
nor provably complete, and latency means today's activity is not visible
yet. These numbers are a reliable picture of usage, not an audit trail —
do not present them as a compliance artifact.

In the raw log data, a vended session with no `caller` tag literally
embeds `anon` in its session name (that's the vending endpoint's own
fallback) -- which is why the query above folds it into `anonymous` rather
than treating "vended but untagged" as its own category. Passing a tag is
what moves a request out of `anonymous` and into an attributable name:

```{r}
#| label: caller-tag

con <- connect_to_s3("cori.data.qcew", caller = "quarterly-refresh")
DBI::dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
```
